questions.q: Which SQL standard standardized the core window-function syntax (OVER/PARTITION BY/ORDER BY)?
options: There is no standard for window functions
questions.explain: Window functions were standardized in SQL:2003, and vendors implemented it closely, making this one of the more portable areas of SQL.

questions.q: How does ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) syntax compare across T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL 8.0+, and PostgreSQL?
options: Nearly identical — the same function names and OVER/PARTITION BY/ORDER BY syntax work almost everywhere
Completely different function names on every platform
Only T-SQL and Oracle support ROW_NUMBER at all
PostgreSQL requires a totally different clause structure
questions.explain: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, and the OVER/PARTITION BY/ORDER BY syntax are part of SQL:2003 and work almost identically across all four dialects in this course.

questions.q: What do LAG and LEAD do?
options: Reach to a previous or following row within the same partition
Group rows into buckets by a column value
Remove duplicate rows from a result set
Convert a column to a different data type
questions.explain: LAG reaches backward and LEAD reaches forward to a row within the same window partition — both are part of the same portable SQL:2003 window-function family.

questions.q: What are the two areas where minor platform-specific window-function variation still exists?
options: Default frame behavior with ORDER BY ties, and advanced frame clause syntax like named windows
The function names ROW_NUMBER and RANK themselves differ by platform
PARTITION BY is not supported on Oracle
Only Oracle supports window functions used as running totals
questions.explain: The core mental model transfers directly everywhere; small variation remains in default frame behavior around ties and in some advanced/extended frame clause syntax (e.g. named windows).

questions.q: How does this lesson's portability compare to what the next chapter (procedural SQL) will show?
options: Window functions are notably MORE portable than procedural SQL, which was never fully standardized
Window functions are notably LESS portable than procedural SQL
Both are equally portable across all dialects
Neither window functions nor procedural SQL have any standard at all
questions.explain: The querying language (joins, CTEs, set operations, window functions) shares a largely common vocabulary; procedural extensions were never fully standardized, which is exactly why T-SQL and PL/SQL diverge sharply in the next chapter.
